sentences.text: learn English for everyday situations. Today, we're going to talk about a very important
topic, how to speak English at the hospital. If you are in an English-speaking country
and need to visit a hospital, knowing basic English phrases will help you communicate
with doctors, nurses, and hospital staff. In this episode, we will learn, one, how to
check in at the hospital, two, how to describe your symptoms, three, how to talk
to a doctor, four, how to understand medical instructions, five, how to ask for
medicine, six, what to do in an emergency, seven, how to leave the hospital and
ask follow-up questions. By the end of this episode, you will feel more confident
speaking English at the hospital. Are you ready? Let's begin. Checking in at the
hospital. When you arrive at the hospital, the first thing you need to do is check
in at the reception desk. The receptionist will ask for your basic
information. The receptionist may ask, what is your full name? Do you have an
appointment? What is your date of birth? Do you have health insurance? What is the
reason for your visit? You can say, my name is Emily Johnson. I don't have an
appointment. My birthday is June 5, 1995. Yes, I have insurance. No, I don't have
insurance. I have a fever and a bad cough. After checking in, you may be asked to
wait in the waiting room until a doctor is ready to see you. Describing your
symptoms. When you see the doctor, you need to explain how you feel. The doctor
may ask, what's wrong? How do you feel? When did your symptoms start? Do you have a
fever? Are you allergic to any medicine? You can say, I have a stomachache and
nausea. I feel very weak and tired. I have had a headache for two days. Yes, I have a
any medicine. Common symptoms vocabulary, headache, pain in your head, fever, high
body temperature, cough when you keep coughing, sore throat, pain in your throat,
runny nose when your nose is dripping, vomiting when you throw up, dizziness,
feeling like you will fall, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, talking to
the doctor. The doctor will ask more questions and give you advice. The doctor
may say, let me check your temperature. I will take your blood pressure. You need to
drink more water and rest. I will prescribe some medicine for you. You may
can ask, is my condition serious? Do I need an x-ray? Can I go home today? Should I
see a specialist? What should I do to feel better? Asking for medicine. If the
doctor gives you a prescription, you need to go to the pharmacy to get your
medicine. The doctor or nurse may say, take this medicine three times a day. Take
one pill after meals. You need antibiotics for five days. This is for pain relief.
You can buy this at the pharmacy. You can ask, how often should I take this? Are
there any side effects? Do I need to take this with food? Where can I find the
pharmacy? Can I take this if I am pregnant? Emergency situations. If you
have a medical emergency, you need to ask for help quickly. If you call an
ambulance, you can say, I need an ambulance. There was an accident. Please come
quickly. The person is unconscious. In the emergency room, you can say, I have
chest pain. I can't breathe. I feel very weak. My friend fainted. Leaving the
hospital. When your treatment is finished, you may need instructions for
recovery. The doctor may say, you need to rest for a few days. Come back for a
checkup next week. Avoid junk food and drink more water. Take your medicine
regularly. You can go home now. You can ask, when can I go back to work? Should I
continue taking medicine? Can I exercise? Do I need another appointment? Can I get a
medical report for work? Useful hospital vocabulary. People in the hospital,
doctor, the person who treats you. Nurse, the person who helps the doctor. Patient,
a sick person in the hospital. Receptionist, the person at the front desk.
Pharmacist, the person who gives medicine. Common medical tools. Thermometer. Measures
your temperature. Stethoscope listens to your heartbeat. Bandage covers a wound,
injection, a shot, or vaccine. Wheelchair helps people move. Places in the
hospital. Emergency room for urgent care. Waiting room where patients wait. Pharmacy
where you get medicine. X-ray room for checking broken bones. ICU intensive care
unit for serious patients. Now you know how to speak English at the hospital.
Final tips. One, stay calm in medical situations. Two, learn common symptoms in
medical words. Always ask questions if you don't understand. I hope this episode
